title: The Art of Composable Primitives
description: >-
  Many of the design principles are aspects of one idea: research software is
  best built from primitives that its callers compose. What makes primitives
  composable, where to cut a method into primitives, and where a composition of
  correct primitives still gives a wrong number, with small examples in Python
  and R.
order: 1

  html: default
  pdf:
    output-file: The_Art_of_Composable_Primitives

Many principles of [](../principles/design.qmd) are aspects of one idea.
Library code provides primitives and leaves the program to its caller. It takes
and returns the data types of the host stack, does not touch global state, does
not modify its arguments, does not print or plot, and does not guess. A method
is built from the primitives of its steps, and the convenient function is a
short composition of them. Each of these is a rule of its own, stated in the
principle where it applies. This essay explains what the rules have in common.

In this essay, a primitive is a unit of code that carries out one step: a
function that removes the baseline of a spectrum, computes a distance matrix,
or fits a model, or a workflow step or a command-line tool that does one job.
To compose primitives is to pass the result of one primitive to the next, in
the caller's code. Primitives are composable when a caller can compose them in
an order and a number that their authors did not foresee, and each primitive
still does what it promises. The essay states no rules; where it refers to a
rule, it cites the principle that states it.


# The next analysis is unknown {#sec-next-analysis}

If the next analysis were known, it would not be research. A package for
spectra will be applied to kinds of spectra that its authors never measured,
used with baseline corrections that they did not implement, and run inside
workflows that they have never seen. No set of options anticipates these
requirements, because they are not known when the package is written. What a
package can provide instead is composable primitives, from which its callers
build the analyses that its authors did not plan.

Composition supports the checks that research applies to its own results. A
reviewer asks whether a result holds under another normalization; an ablation
study removes one step of a method at a time; a sensitivity analysis varies one
step and holds the others fixed. If the method is a composition of primitives,
each of these checks replaces one primitive in the caller's code. If the method
is one block, each check requires a copy of the package's code, which then
drifts from the original ([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-dry)).

Composition also makes correctness checkable. A primitive that carries out one
step can be checked against one equation, and known answers exist mostly for
such small steps ([](../principles/testing.qmd#sec-known-answers)). A
composition of checked primitives can then be verified line by line, and a
failing test identifies the primitive that broke. One block can be checked only
as a whole, against the few cases in which the answer for the whole method is
known.


# Primitives, composition, abstraction {#sec-mechanisms}

*Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs*, by Abelson and Sussman,
opens with the three mechanisms that every powerful language has: primitive
expressions, which are the simplest entities; means of combination, by which
compound elements are built from simpler ones; and means of abstraction, by
which compound elements are named and used as units. The same three mechanisms
describe a package of research software, with composition in the place of
combination:

- **Primitives** are the steps of the method, as functions or as workflow
  steps, together with the functions of the host stack that the package uses.
- **Composition** takes place in the caller's code: a script, a notebook, a
  shell pipeline, a workflow.
- **Abstraction** gives a name to a composition that callers need often, such
  as a convenient function, a command, or a workflow. The named composition is
  a primitive of the layer above ([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-layers)).

The three mechanisms work together because of what the book calls the closure
property: the result of a composition is of the same kind as its arguments, so
it can be composed again. The ufuncs of NumPy and the vectorized functions of R
take arrays and return arrays, so their calls can be nested. The verbs of dplyr
take a data frame and return a data frame, so they can be chained with `|>`, as
the methods of pandas and Polars can be chained with a dot. A `Pipeline` of
scikit-learn is itself an estimator, so it can be passed to a grid search or
included in another pipeline. A Unix pipeline reads and writes streams as each
of its commands does, and a subworkflow of Nextflow is called like a single
process. A package has the closure property when the results of its primitives
are valid arguments of its primitives.


# What makes primitives composable {#sec-composable}

Primitives that are correct individually are not necessarily composable. Six
properties make them composable, and each property is the subject of one or
more principles.


## Common data types {#sec-data-types}

Primitives are composable when the result of one primitive is a valid argument
of the next, without conversion. The data types that make this possible at the
lowest cost are those of the host stack: its arrays and data frames, including
sparse, lazy, and chunked ones, which the other packages of the host stack also
take and return ([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-follow-types)). Every data
type that a package introduces is accepted only by that package, and every
caller has to write glue code to convert it. A data type of the package is
justified where it protects an invariant, as a fitted model does, and it costs
its callers least when it converts to the data types of the host stack and
back.

A data type that inherits from a data type of the host stack claims to be that
data type, with every operation and every convention of the original. If it
does not keep all of them, code written for the original runs on it and gives
a different result. For this reason, the Liskov principle prefers wrapping a
data type of the host stack to inheriting from it
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-substitution)).


## No hidden inputs {#sec-hidden-inputs}

A primitive is composable when its result depends only on its arguments. Every
other input is a hidden input: the global random number generator, a setting at
module level, a variable that another function sets, a file at a fixed path. A
hidden input makes the result of a primitive depend on what ran before it in
the same process, so that the result of a composition depends on more than the
composition. Two primitives that draw from the global random number generator
return different numbers when they are called in the opposite order, and two
analyses in the same session change each other's results.

The principles remove the hidden inputs. Randomness enters as an argument, a
generator or a seed that the caller passes
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-reproducibility)), and the modules of a
package depend on each other only through what they promise
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-modules)). A primitive without hidden inputs
is also the simplest to test: the test passes the arguments and checks the
result, and nothing else has to be set up
([](../principles/testing.qmd#sec-isolated)).


## No side effects {#sec-side-effects}

A primitive is composable when its return value is its only effect. Every other
effect is a side effect: modifying an argument, changing a setting of the
process, printing, plotting, writing a file. A return value can still be
printed, plotted, written to a file, tested, or passed to the next primitive;
a printed value can only be read. A side effect also removes a decision from
the caller: where a figure or a file goes, in which format, and whether it is
produced at all.

The principles remove the side effects from library code. Library code leaves
the settings of the process unchanged
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-global-state)), returns new data instead of
modifying its arguments ([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-mutation)), does no
work when it is loaded ([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-import)), and leaves
reading and writing files to its caller
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-no-files)). It returns results that separate
functions plot ([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-plotting)), and it reports
problems through the warnings and errors of the host stack, which the caller
controls ([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-output)). Side effects belong in
workflow code, which owns the program and its output.


## Mechanism, not policy {#sec-mechanism}

*The Art of Unix Programming*, by Eric Raymond, states a rule of separation:
separate policy from mechanism. Mechanism is what a primitive can do, such as
smoothing a signal with a window of any width; policy is what an analysis does
with the mechanism, such as smoothing with a window of eleven samples.
Mechanism is composable, because any policy can be built on it. Policy is not,
because the next analysis requires a different policy.

In research software, policy consists of the scientific choices: thresholds,
normalizations, which outliers to remove, how to treat missing values. A
primitive takes these choices as arguments and leaves them to the caller,
instead of making them internally ([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-explicit))
or inferring them from the data ([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-no-guess)). A
default is a policy that the API offers without imposing it, and it is part of
the API ([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-numeric-defaults)). Library code is
mechanism; workflow code, with its configuration, is policy.


## The caller owns the program {#sec-caller-program}

Where a method needs code from its caller, such as an objective function or the
right-hand side of a differential equation, library code takes that code as a
function argument and calls it, as `scipy.optimize.minimize(fun, x0)` in Python
and `optim(par, fn)` in R do. The caller's function remains an ordinary
function, which the caller can test on its own, reuse, and pass to another
optimizer.

A framework inverts this relation. It owns the program, including the solver or
simulation loop, requires its caller to subclass its classes or to register
code with it, and calls that code at points that it determines
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-library)). Library code is composable with
other library code, because each is called and returns. Two frameworks are not
composable, because each requires ownership of the program, and code written
for one does not run in the other. A plugin is code written for a host
application that owns the program, with the disadvantages that
[](../principles/design.qmd#sec-plugins) describes.


## The same conventions in every primitive {#sec-same-conventions}

Primitives that agree on data types can still disagree on conventions. One
primitive puts time on the first axis and the next one on the last; one takes
angles in degrees and the next one returns radians; one counts the positions on
a genome from 0 and the next one from 1; one removes missing values and the
next one propagates them. A composition of such primitives runs without an
error and gives a plausible wrong number
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-loud)).

In a package whose primitives are composable, every primitive uses the same
axis order, the same units, and the same argument names, so that a caller who
knows the conventions of one primitive knows those of all
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-conventions)), and every primitive treats
missing values in the same way ([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-missing)).
Between packages, the conventions of the host stack apply, and a primitive that
replaces another keeps all conventions of the original.


# Options multiply, primitives add {#sec-options}

The usual way to make a function serve more analyses is to add an option. Each
option appears inexpensive, but options multiply: a function with five options
that can be on or off has 32 behaviors, each of which needs documentation and a
test, and the interactions of the options are decided inside the function,
where the caller cannot see them. Is the baseline removed before or after
smoothing? Is the normalization applied to the smoothed spectrum or to the raw
spectrum? And the function still cannot do what its authors did not foresee: a
caller who requires another smoother needs a sixth option.

Primitives add instead. Five steps are five primitives, each tested on its own;
their order is written in the caller's code, where a reader sees it; and a
primitive of the caller's own replaces one of them without a change to the
package. The following example implements a peak finder for spectra in both
ways, first in Python and then in R:

```python
# Options: each combination of options is a path inside the function.
peaks = detect_peaks(spectrum, baseline=True, smooth=True, normalize=True)

# Primitives: the caller determines the order and chooses the smoother.
s = remove_baseline(spectrum)
s = scipy.signal.savgol_filter(s, window_length=11, polyorder=3)
peaks = detect_peaks(normalize(s))
```

```r
# Options: each combination of options is a path inside the function.
peaks <- detect_peaks(spectrum, baseline = TRUE, smooth = TRUE,
                      normalize = TRUE)

# Primitives: the caller determines the order and chooses the smoother.
peaks <- spectrum |>
  remove_baseline() |>
  signal::sgolayfilt(p = 3, n = 11) |>
  normalize() |>
  detect_peaks()
```

This is not an argument against options. The convenient function in the top
layer keeps a few options for the common case, provided that it is a short
composition of public primitives: a caller whose analysis it does not cover
then uses the layer below instead of copying its implementation
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-layers)). The warning sign is an option added
for a single caller, which [](../principles/design.qmd#sec-wrong-abstraction)
describes as the mark of a wrong abstraction.


# Cut where the paper cuts {#sec-cut}

The central design decision is where to cut a method into primitives, and the
method itself indicates where. The steps that a methods section lists and the
equations that a paper numbers are the steps that a reader of the paper can
check and that a caller is likely to replace
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-ground-up)). The steps that callers replace
most often justify a primitive of their own even when they are small: the
weighting, the kernel, the distance, the mask, the prior.

A good cut meets three criteria. The primitive has a name that denotes a
concept of the field, such as baseline, distance matrix, or posterior, not a
name that describes its position in the code, such as `preprocess2` or
`helper`. Its arguments and its result are quantities of the field, such as a
spectrum or a list of peaks, not internal state, such as a buffer that only the
next primitive can interpret. And it has a known answer of its own.

A cut can also be wrong. Two primitives that are always called together, in the
same order, and whose intermediate result has no meaning on its own are one
step cut in two: every caller has to repeat the pair and can call it in the
wrong order. Cutting finer than the steps of the method adds names without
adding choices ([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-kiss)), and every public
primitive is a commitment ([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-stable-api)), which
is why primitives may remain internal until callers need them.

Callers reveal where a cut is missing. When they copy the implementation of a
function into their own code to change one line of it, a primitive is missing
below that function. When they write glue code to convert the result of one
primitive of the package into an argument of another, a common data type is
missing. And when they request an option, they often need a primitive.


# Correct primitives, wrong composition {#sec-wrong-composition}

Composition has a limit that is specific to numerical code: a composition of
correct primitives can give a wrong result. The variance is the mean of the
squares minus the square of the mean, and both means are computed correctly in
the following code, first in Python and then in R:

```python
x = 1e9 + np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
np.mean(x**2) - np.mean(x)**2    # 0.0
np.mean((x - np.mean(x))**2)     # 0.6666666666666666
```

```r
x <- 1e9 + c(1, 2, 3)
mean(x^2) - mean(x)^2            # 0
mean((x - mean(x))^2)            # 0.6666667
```

The squares lie near $10^{18}$, where adjacent floating-point numbers are 128
apart, and their difference of 2/3 is lost in the subtraction. The second line
composes the same primitives in a different order, centering before squaring,
and is accurate. The choice is therefore not between composition and no
composition, but between compositions. Some compositions are so common and so
unstable that the host stacks provide them as primitives of their own:
`log1p(x)` for `log(1 + x)`, `expm1(x)` for `exp(x) - 1`, and `logsumexp` in
SciPy or `logSumExp` in the R package matrixStats for `log(sum(exp(x)))`
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-stability)). These functions are not
shortcuts: the fused function is the correct primitive, and the composition
that it replaces is the defect. Composing well therefore includes recognizing a
composition that has to be a primitive.

Errors also propagate through a composition. Each primitive can be accurate to
its tolerance while the composition is not, because a later primitive amplifies
the error of an earlier one to the extent that its problem is ill-conditioned
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-convergence)). A tolerance that holds for each
primitive therefore says little about their composition, which needs a test and
a tolerance of its own ([](../principles/testing.qmd#sec-float-tests)).

Composition also has a cost in time and memory: each primitive materializes its
intermediate result, which a fused function does not store. Fusing primitives
into one function is therefore a legitimate optimization, and the composition
of the primitives remains useful as a second opinion for the fused function
([](../principles/testing.qmd#sec-second-opinion)). In either form, expensive
operations remain visible in the caller's code
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-cost)).


# Workflow steps are primitives too {#sec-workflows}

The Unix philosophy, in the words of Doug McIlroy: write programs that do one
thing and do it well; write programs to work together; write programs to handle
text streams, because that is a universal interface. The first two sentences
hold unchanged for the steps of a research workflow. The third has a research
form: the universal interfaces are the standard file formats of a field, such
as BAM, NetCDF, or Parquet, and a workflow step that reads and writes them is
composable with every other tool that reads and writes them
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-hand-off)). The properties of @sec-composable
carry over to workflow steps: a file that a step reads without declaring it is
a hidden input, and a file that it writes without declaring it is a side effect
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-declared-inputs)). The workflow manager
composes the steps as a shell composes commands.

The division between library code and workflow code recurs inside each
workflow step. A command-line tool that does one job is library code behind a
thin layer of workflow code ([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-package)), an
arrangement that Gary Bernhardt named *functional core, imperative shell*. The
core computes, from arguments to return values, and is simple to test and to
compose. The shell parses the command-line arguments, reads and writes the
files, and writes the log, and it remains thin enough to be checked by running
it on a small dataset ([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-end-to-end)). The
properties that make the core composable are the properties that keep the shell
thin.


# Questions to ask of a primitive {#sec-questions}

Composability becomes evident in use, so a primitive is best examined by
calling it as its callers will. The following questions reveal most defects
before a caller encounters them:

- Can it be called twice in succession, with the same result both times?
- Can it be called on a subset of the data, on one chunk, or in parallel with
  itself?
- Does it run without reading or writing a file, and without printing or
  plotting?
- Can it be called from a test, with nothing set up except its arguments?
- Can its result be passed to the next primitive of the package without
  conversion?
- If it is a composition of other primitives, can a caller replace one of them
  without copying the others?
- Does its name denote a concept of the field?
- Is every quantity that affects its result an argument?

A negative answer indicates that one of the properties of @sec-composable is
missing, or that the cut is in the wrong place (@sec-cut).
